The Story of the Palm Frond

From desert shelter to written souvenir: how the UAE's "tree of life" shaped daily life, craft and identity

c. 7,000 years agoPalm-based building traced in the region
2600 to 2000 BCEUmm an-Nar culture, date palm remains vital
Early 1900s to 1950sPeak of arish living and everyday khoos crafts
2000s to 2010sWorkshops, festivals and heritage centres revive khoos
2019UNESCO recognises date palm traditions

Look at a palm tree in the UAE and you are looking at a house, a dining mat, a hand fan, a bag and a hat, all waiting to be made. For thousands of years, people in this land survived the desert heat by learning to use every part of the date palm. The fronds, called khoos, became the raw material of a craft that is still alive today. Follow the timeline below, from the first palm-leaf homes to the personalised souvenirs you can buy now.

About 7,000 years ago to the 1st century AD

1Roots: A Tree That Built a Civilisation

Overviewc. 3000 BCEWhere did the idea come from?

Long before the UAE existed, the date palm was already the centre of life here. It gave shade, food, wood, fibre and leaves in a land with very little else.

c. 7,000 years agoStudies cited by architect Sandra Piesik trace palm-based building in the region back about 7,000 years. One example is a very early house made from palm trunks at an archaeological site on Delma Island, Abu Dhabi.
c. 3000 BCEThe earliest evidence of crop growing in the UAE comes from Hili in Al Ain, and the date palm was one of the important crops. In the Umm an-Nar culture (about 2600 to 2000 BCE), the date palm remained just as important.
1st century BCE to 1st century ADArchaeologists believe the living quarters at the trading site of ed-Dur in Umm Al Quwain were arish, which are palm-frond dwellings. Microscopic palm remains were also found there.

Where did the idea come from?

No single inventor is recorded. The idea grew out of necessity. Fronds were everywhere, they were light, they dried hard in the sun, and they let air pass through. Early communities noticed that a roof or wall of fronds kept the summer heat off while staying breezy. Over generations, families discovered that the same leaves could be split, dried and braided into containers, mats and ropes. Skills were taught by watching and doing, from mother to daughter and from mother-in-law to bride.

Did you know? Each date palm can drop 10 to 25 dried fronds a year, and the UAE has an estimated 42 million date palms. That is a huge natural resource.

Early 20th century to the 1950s

2Life Before Oil: Every Part of the Palm

OverviewThe palm-frond houseHow khoos was preparedThe dining matThe hand fanFood containers and coversHats, bags and everyday tools

Before oil, the palm was a lifeline. Heritage authorities describe how Emirati families benefited from every part of the tree, and the weaving of fronds is called Al Khous (also written Khoos). A related technique, safeefah, is the weaving of the dried fronds into finished items.

The palm-frond house (arish or barasti)

Summer homesBedouin families lived in tents of goat or camel hair in winter and in arish shelters in the hot months. A frame of mangrove poles or split palm trunks was covered with fronds, as screens that let air flow and as roof thatch.
1950sDubai had as many as 4,000 arish houses, home to about 12,000 people, and Liwa once had around 800. Building one was a community effort.

How khoos was prepared

Fronds were plucked and left in the sun to harden, for about a week in summer and up to a month in winter. They were then cleaned, split into strips, softened in water and sewn with a needle. Strips were dyed by dipping them in hot coloured water, in natural shades such as purple, green and red, then dried again. Weavers often combine coloured and natural strips to create patterns.

What people made, and why

The dining mat (sufra)Families ate seated on the floor. Woven mats were used for sleeping and for placing food trays, and tablecloth-style mats served as the dining surface. This is the palm-frond "dining table" of the past. Plates and trays sat on it, so it needed to be flat, clean and washable by brushing.
The hand fanWith no air conditioning, a palm-frond fan was an everyday cooling tool. Its open weave moves air while staying light enough to hold for hours. Fans are one of the best-known khoos objects.
Food containers and coversCovered baskets and bowls kept bread and dates, and date-basket covers protected stored fruit. The weave let food breathe, which helped it keep fresh in the heat.
Hats, bags and everyday toolsHats shaded workers in the farm and on the shore. Bags were made to be carried by camels. Brooms, mats, ropes and even miniature boats were also made from palm material.
Did you know? Women are most associated with this craft in the Gulf, but Sharjah Institute for Heritage notes that men can weave safeefah too.

Late 1950s to 2019

3Change and Revival: From Need to Heritage

Overview2000s to 2010s2018 to 2021 and 2019

After oil was discovered in the late 1950s, life changed quickly. Concrete homes replaced arish, and plastic and metal replaced many woven goods. The craft nearly moved from "everyday need" to "memory". Then communities, museums and government bodies began to protect it as intangible heritage.

Late 1950s onwardThe popularity of arish architecture declined after the discovery of oil, and modern materials replaced many household items.
2000s to 2010sWorkshops and festivals revived the skill. Al Ain Palace Museum runs interactive craft workshops where local women teach khoos weaving. The Liwa Date Festival celebrates the palm and all its uses, with women weaving and selling crafts. Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council trains artisans in safeefah through its Bidwa programme. In Dubai, the Centre for Traditional Handicrafts and Heritage in Al Shindagha shows khoos patterns and runs workshops.
2018 and 2021Dubai Culture documented Al Khous during its heritage week in 2018. At the 18th Sharjah Heritage Days in 2021, Emirati women from Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah wove safeefah live for younger Emiratis and expatriates, and the products were sold as decor and souvenirs.
2019UNESCO inscribed the traditions and skills of the date palm, shared by several countries including the UAE, on its Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

Present day

4Today and Tomorrow: Palm Craft and Written Souvenirs

OverviewWritten souvenirsThree linksTry it yourself

Today the palm frond has a double life. It is a respected heritage craft, and it is also a design material for modern homes, gifts and architecture. Fans, baskets, trays, bags and decorative pieces are sold at heritage souks and festivals. Architects are exploring palm-leaf building again as a sustainable idea, for example the Sabla Project's domes made from bundled fronds.

Written souvenirs: the new trend

A growing souvenir trend adds writing to palm craft: a name, a short phrase, or Arabic calligraphy placed on a woven item or a palm-frond piece such as a bookmark, coaster, tag or small basket. The writing is the new part. The object, the material and the weaving are the old part. That is why the trend matters for heritage.

Link 1: Same materialThe souvenir still starts with khoos, so the craft, the dyeing and the weaving skills are kept in use.
Link 2: Same purposePalm crafts have always carried a household's identity. A written name makes that personal link visible, and a visitor carries a piece of Emirati culture home.
Link 3: Support for makersWhen visitors and residents buy from heritage centres and women artisans, the craft earns an income, which gives young people a reason to learn it.

Try it yourself (for Alpha explorers)

Ask a weaver to show you how a strip of khoos is split and braided. Then try a simple braid with paper strips at home. Look for the weave in fans, baskets and mats on your next visit to a museum or souk, and ask who made it.

Remember: every woven souvenir is a small piece of a 7,000-year story. Choose items made by local artisans and ask about the maker.

Glossary

Date palm

The centre of life here. It gave shade, food, wood, fibre and leaves in a land with very little else.

Khoos (Al Khous)

The fronds of the date palm and the craft of weaving them.

Safeefah

The weaving of the dried fronds into finished items.

Arish (barasti)

A palm-frond dwelling: a frame of mangrove poles or split palm trunks covered with fronds.

Sufra

The woven dining mat. Families ate seated on the floor, and food trays were placed on it.

Mahafah

The palm-frond hand fan, an everyday cooling tool.

Makabah

A woven food cover.

Jefeer

A basket for carrying dates.
